Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
42-year-old woman with sudden‐onset continuous spinning vertigo, ear buzzing, and nausea × 2 h; no focal neurologic signs. Clinical impression: acute vestibular neuritis / labyrinthitis.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Continuous vertigo (“room spinning”) with nausea and ear buzzing.  
• Onset/duration: Began abruptly 2 h ago while making breakfast; persists unchanged. Similar brief self-resolving episode 1 mo ago (5–10 min).  
• Associated symptoms: Unsteady gait; feels shaky. No vomiting, headache, ear pain, discharge, fever, recent URI, or limb weakness. Hearing intact.  
• Pertinent negatives: No recent infection, no focal neuro deficits, no vision change.  
• PMH: Premature ovarian failure; on hormone replacement therapy.  
• Medications: HRT only.  
• Allergies: Denies drug allergies.  
• Social/preventive: Married; other social history not discussed.

Examination:
(Conducted via video; no vitals taken.)  
• General: Appears dizzy but conversational.  
• Neurologic (subjective): Normal limb strength; ambulates but veers due to vertigo. No reported facial asymmetry, speech disturbance, or limb numbness.  
• ENT (subjective): Tinnitus; no otalgia, otorrhea, or hearing loss.

Impression:
Most likely: Acute vestibular neuritis / viral labyrinthitis—sudden continuous vertigo, tinnitus, gait unsteadiness, absence of focal deficits or hearing loss.  
Alternate considerations:  
1. Ménière’s disease – recurrent vertigo and tinnitus, but lacks fluctuating hearing loss.  
2. Posterior-circulation stroke/TIA – low probability given age, no risk factors, and normal neuro screen; advised red-flag monitoring.

Plan:
• Symptomatic therapy: Prescription sent electronically to local Lloyds pharmacy—one tablet TID for 10 days (anti-vertigo/anti-emetic; name not specified in transcript).  
• Follow-up: Arrange face-to-face appointment within next few days for full ENT and neurologic exam, including otoscopy and blood pressure measurement.  
• Safety-net advice: Attend ED immediately if new limb weakness, severe headache, or persistent vomiting develops.  
• Patient instructed to contact support to book the follow-up visit; agreed to plan and had no further questions.

Quality checks:

● Missing/expected data:
  – Drug name and dose not captured in transcript.  
  – No vital signs, formal neuro exam, or blood glucose.  
  – Social history (smoking, alcohol), family history, vaccination status not elicited.  
  – Explicit follow-up date/time not set.

● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  – None; both align on vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis as leading diagnosis.

● Transcript quality:
  – Clear but lacks objective exam and medication details; occasional audio gaps (e.g., drug name unintelligible).
